title: Der Jude im Dorn
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 110. Text from Wikisource („Der Jude im Dorn (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 110 is the most openly antisemitic tale in the Grimms' collection, and its central device is a magic fiddle turned into a weapon. A servant cheated of three years' wages gives the little he has to a dwarf and receives in return a gun that never misses, a fiddle that forces anyone within earshot to dance, and the power that no request of his can ever be refused. He shoots a bird into a thornbush for a Jew he meets on the road, sends the man in after it, and then fiddles him into a helpless, bleeding dance among the thorns until he pays a bag of gold to be let stop. The Jew's honest complaint to a judge is dismissed out of hand — the tale states as plain fact that no Jew would ever part with money willingly — and the servant is condemned to hang; his last request, the fiddle once more, sets the whole courtroom dancing until the judge frees him and, at fiddle-point, forces the Jew himself to ‘confess’ to theft, whereupon the judge has him hanged in the servant's place.

advisory.lede: This tale is openly antisemitic: a Jew is tormented, robbed and hanged, and the story is told as a comedy.
advisory.more: Der Jude im Dorn stood in every edition of the Kinder- und Hausmärchen from 1815 onward. Its Jewish character is assembled wholly out of the stereotypes of the Grimms’ Germany — grasping, cringing, dishonest — and the tale’s sympathy rests entirely with the servant who fiddles him bloody in a thorn hedge, takes his purse, and then watches him hang on a charge the reader knows to be false. The contempt is not period colour around the edges of the plot; it is the plot. Lectorium presents the text unaltered, as the historical document it is, and the notes name the stereotypes where they drive the action rather than passing over them.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein reicher Mann, der hatte einen Knecht, der diente ihm fleißig und redlich, war alle Morgen der erste aus dem Bett und Abends der letzte hinein, und wenns eine saure Arbeit gab, wo keiner anpacken wollte, so stellte er sich immer zuerst daran.
sentences.l: There was once a rich man; he had a servant who served him diligently and honestly, was every morning the first out of bed and in the evening the last in, and if there was a sour piece of work that nobody wanted to lay hands on, he always set himself to it first.
sentences.i: There was once a rich man who had a servant that served him diligently and honestly: he was the first out of bed every morning and the last into it at night, and whenever there was a hard piece of work that no one would take hold of, he was always the first to set to it.
sentences.n: “der hatte einen Knecht” picks the man up again with a demonstrative der, spoken German’s way of stringing clauses together. “der letzte hinein” leaves the verb out altogether, the direction word doing all the work: the last [in]to bed. saure Arbeit is heavy, disagreeable work. wenns = wenn es.

sentences.t: Dabei klagte er nicht, sondern war mit allem zufrieden, und war immer lustig.
sentences.l: With that he did not complain, but was content with everything, and was always merry.
sentences.i: For all that he did not complain, but was content with everything and always merry.
sentences.n: dabei is literally with it, alongside that, and here concessive: for all that.

sentences.t: Als sein Jahr herum war, gab ihm der Herr keinen Lohn und dachte „das ist das gescheidtste, so spare ich etwas, und er geht mir nicht weg, sondern bleibt hübsch im Dienst.“
sentences.l: When his year was round, the master gave him no wages and thought “that is the cleverest thing, so I save something, and he does not go away on me, but stays nicely in service.”
sentences.i: When his year was up, the master gave him no wages, and thought: “That is the cleverest course: I save something, and he does not walk off on me but stays nicely in service.”
sentences.n: “herum sein,” of time, is to be up, to be over. gescheidtste is the 1857 spelling of gescheiteste. The mir in “geht mir nicht weg” is the dative of the person concerned in the matter, which English can only render as on me. Farm service was hired and paid by the year.

sentences.t: Der Knecht schwieg auch still, that das zweite Jahr wie das erste seine Arbeit, und als er am Ende desselben abermals keinen Lohn bekam, ließ er sichs gefallen und blieb noch länger.
sentences.l: The servant kept silent too, did the second year his work as the first, and when at the end of the same he again received no wages, he let it please him and stayed longer still.
sentences.i: The servant held his peace, did his work the second year as he had the first, and when at the end of it he again got no wages, he put up with it and stayed on longer still.
sentences.n: stillschweigen is to keep silent; that is the 1857 spelling of tat, from thun/tun. “sich etwas gefallen lassen” — to let a thing please one — is to put up with it. desselben, of the same, means of that year.

sentences.t: Als auch das dritte Jahr herum war, bedachte sich der Herr, griff in die Tasche, holte aber nichts heraus.
sentences.l: When the third year too was round, the master bethought himself, reached into his pocket, but brought nothing out.
sentences.i: When the third year too was up, the master considered a while, put his hand in his pocket — but brought nothing out of it.
sentences.n: “sich bedenken” is to think a thing over, to hesitate. herausholen is separable, its particle at the end. The gesture without the coin is the whole character.

sentences.t: Da fieng der Knecht endlich an und sprach „Herr, ich habe euch drei Jahre redlich gedient, seid so gut und gebt mir was mir von Rechtswegen zukommt: ich wollte fort und mich gerne weiter in der Welt umsehen.“
sentences.l: Then the servant at last began and spoke “master, I have served you three years honestly, be so good and give me what is due to me by rights: I wanted to be off and to look about me further in the world.”
sentences.i: Then at last the servant began, and said: “Master, I have served you honestly for three years; be so good as to give me what is mine by right. I should like to be off and to see something more of the world.”
sentences.n: fieng an is the 1857 spelling of fing an, from separable anfangen. “von Rechtswegen” is by rights, as a matter of law. zukommen, to be due to someone, takes the dative. “ich wollte” is the past subjunctive used for politeness: I should like.

sentences.t: Da antwortete der Geizhals „ja, mein lieber Knecht, du hast mir unverdrossen gedient, dafür sollst du mildiglich belohnet werden,“
sentences.l: Then the skinflint answered “yes, my dear servant, you have served me untiringly, and for that you shall be bountifully rewarded,”
sentences.i: Then the miser answered: “Yes, my dear servant, you have served me without a murmur, and for that you shall be handsomely rewarded,”
sentences.n: The narrator drops Geizhals — greed-throat, skinflint — into the speech tag, so the master is judged before he opens his mouth. mildiglich is an old adverb, graciously, bountifully, and belohnet the older spelling of belohnt; the solemn, generous ring of both is the joke.

sentences.t: griff abermals in die Tasche und zählte dem Knecht drei Heller einzeln auf, „da hast du für jedes Jahr einen Heller, das ist ein großer und reichlicher Lohn, wie du ihn bei wenigen Herrn empfangen hättest.“
sentences.l: reached into his pocket again and counted the servant out three Heller one by one, “there you have a Heller for each year, that is a great and ample wage, such as you would have received from few masters.”
sentences.i: put his hand in his pocket again and counted the servant out three hellers one by one: “There you have a heller for each year — that is a great and ample wage, such as you would have got from few masters.”
sentences.n: The Heller is the smallest copper coin there is: three of them for three years of work. aufzählen, to count out, is separable, with the auf at the end. hättest is past subjunctive: would have.

sentences.t: Der gute Knecht, der vom Geld wenig verstand, strich sein Capital ein und dachte „nun hast du vollauf in der Tasche, was willst du sorgen und dich mit schwerer Arbeit länger plagen.“
sentences.l: The good servant, who understood little of money, raked his capital in and thought “now you have plenty in your pocket, why should you worry and plague yourself with heavy work any longer.”
sentences.i: The good servant, who knew little about money, pocketed his capital and thought: “Now you have plenty in your pocket; why trouble yourself and toil at heavy work any longer?”
sentences.n: einstreichen, to rake in or pocket, is separable, and the ein stands at the end. Capital, the older spelling of Kapital, is far too grand a word for three coppers, which is why it is used. He addresses himself as du; was here is why.

sentences.t: Da zog er fort, bergauf, bergab, sang und sprang nach Herzenslust.
sentences.l: Then he moved off, uphill, downhill, sang and sprang to his heart’s content.
sentences.i: So he went off, uphill and downhill, singing and leaping to his heart’s content.
sentences.n: fortziehen, to move off, is separable. “nach Herzenslust” is as the heart desires.

sentences.t: Nun trug es sich zu, als er an ein Buschwerk vorüber kam, daß ein kleines Männchen hervortrat und ihn anrief „wo hinaus, Bruder Lustig?
sentences.l: Now it came about, as he came past a thicket, that a little manikin stepped forth and called to him “where away, Brother Merry?
sentences.i: Now it came about, as he was passing a thicket, that a little man stepped out and hailed him: “Where away, Brother Merry?
sentences.n: “sich zutragen” is to come to pass. hervortreten, vorüberkommen and anrufen are all separable. “wo hinaus” — where out to — is the old way of asking where a man is bound. Bruder Lustig is a stock name for a cheerful vagabond, and another tale in the collection (KHM 81) is called after him.

sentences.t: ich sehe du trägst nicht schwer an deinen Sorgen.“
sentences.l: I see you do not carry heavily at your cares.”
sentences.i: I see your cares do not weigh on you heavily.”
sentences.n: “an etwas schwer tragen” — to carry heavy at something — is to be weighed down by it. The daß after ich sehe is simply left out, as German freely leaves it out.

sentences.t: „Was soll ich traurig sein,“ antwortete der Knecht, „ich habe vollauf, der Lohn von drei Jahren klingelt in meiner Tasche.“
sentences.l: “Why should I be sad,” answered the servant, “I have plenty, the wages of three years jingle in my pocket.”
sentences.i: “Why should I be sad?” answered the servant. “I have plenty: three years’ wages jingle in my pocket.”
sentences.n: was = why once more. klingeln, of coins, is to jingle — three coppers would not, and the reader is meant to hear that they do not.

sentences.t: „Wie viel ist denn deines Schatzes?“ fragte ihn das Männchen.
sentences.l: “How much is there of your treasure, then?” the manikin asked him.
sentences.i: “And how much is your treasure?” the little man asked him.
sentences.n: An old genitive turn: “wie viel ist … deines Schatzes,” how much is there of your treasure. denn in a question is the small untranslatable word of curiosity: then, now.

sentences.t: „Wie viel? drei baare Heller, richtig gezählt.“
sentences.l: “How much? three Heller in cash, rightly counted.”
sentences.i: “How much? Three hellers in ready money, counted true.”
sentences.n: baare (modern bar) is in cash, coin in hand. “richtig gezählt” — counted correct — is the small boast of a man with three coppers.

sentences.t: „Höre,“ sagte der Zwerg, „ich bin ein armer bedürftiger Mann, schenke mir deine drei Heller: ich kann nichts mehr arbeiten, du aber bist jung und kannst dir dein Brot leicht verdienen.“
sentences.l: “Listen,” said the dwarf, “I am a poor needy man, make me a present of your three Heller: I can work no more, but you are young and can earn your bread easily.”
sentences.i: “Listen,” said the dwarf, “I am a poor needy man: give me your three hellers. I can work no longer, but you are young and can easily earn your bread.”
sentences.n: The little man is called Männchen and Zwerg by turns and the tale makes no distinction between them. schenken is to give outright, with nothing expected back.

sentences.t: Und weil der Knecht ein gutes Herz hatte und Mitleid mit dem Männchen fühlte, so reichte er ihm seine drei Heller und sprach „in Gottes Namen, es wird mir doch nicht fehlen.“
sentences.l: And because the servant had a good heart and felt pity with the manikin, so he handed him his three Heller and spoke “in God’s name, it will not be lacking to me.”
sentences.i: And because the servant had a good heart and felt pity for the little man, he handed him his three hellers and said: “In God’s name — I shall not want for it.”
sentences.n: The so at the head of the main clause after weil is the old resumptive, which English drops. “es wird mir nicht fehlen” has the person who would go short in the dative: it will not be lacking to me.

sentences.t: Da sprach das Männchen „weil ich dein gutes Herz sehe, so gewähre ich dir drei Wünsche, für jeden Heller einen, die sollen dir in Erfüllung gehen.“
sentences.l: Then the manikin spoke “because I see your good heart, I grant you three wishes, one for each Heller, and they shall go into fulfilment for you.”
sentences.i: Then the little man said: “Because I see your good heart, I grant you three wishes, one for each heller, and they shall be fulfilled for you.”
sentences.n: “in Erfüllung gehen” — to go into fulfilment — is to come true. The bargain is exact: one wish for each coin.

sentences.t: „Aha,“ sprach der Knecht, „du bist einer, der blau pfeifen kann.
sentences.l: “Aha,” spoke the servant, “you are one who can whistle blue.
sentences.i: “Aha,” said the servant, “you are one of those who can whistle blue.
sentences.n: “blau pfeifen” is not a standing German phrase, and its force here has to be read off the situation: blau in old usage marks the fantastical or the humbug, so the servant is half saying you are a wonder-worker and half saying you are talking nonsense. Any single English rendering picks one of the two, so the literal is left standing.

sentences.t: Wohlan, wenns doch sein soll, so wünsche ich mir erstlich ein Vogelrohr, das alles trifft, wonach ich ziele:
sentences.l: Well then, if it is to be so, I wish myself firstly a bird-gun that hits everything I aim at:
sentences.i: Well then, if it must be so, I wish first for a fowling piece that hits everything I aim at;
sentences.n: Wohlan is an elevated old well then. Das Vogelrohr, bird-tube, is the light gun for shooting birds — Rohr in this tale is always the barrel and so the gun, never the reed. zielen takes nach or auf: wonach ich ziele, what I aim at.

sentences.t: zweitens eine Fidel, wenn ich darauf streiche, so muß alles tanzen, was den Klang hört:
sentences.l: secondly a fiddle — when I draw the bow across it, then everything that hears the sound must dance:
sentences.n: streichen, of a fiddle, is to draw the bow, the same verb as to stroke or to spread; der Strich, further on, is one stroke of that bow. alles is everything and everyone alike, which is exactly what happens.

sentences.t: und drittens, wenn ich an jemand eine Bitte thue, so darf er sie nicht abschlagen.“
sentences.l: and thirdly, when I make a request of somebody, then he may not refuse it.”
sentences.i: and thirdly, when I make a request of anyone, he shall not be able to refuse it.”
sentences.n: “eine Bitte an jemand thun” is to make a request of someone; thue is the 1857 spelling of tue. dürfen here is may in the sense of shall not be permitted — the wish binds the other man. abschlagen is to refuse, to deny a request.

sentences.t: „Das sollst du alles haben“ sprach das Männchen, griff in den Busch, und, denk einer, da lag schon Fidel und Vogelrohr in Bereitschaft, als wenn sie bestellt wären.
sentences.l: “All that you shall have,” spoke the manikin, reached into the bush, and — just think — there lay fiddle and bird-gun already in readiness, as if they had been ordered.
sentences.i: “You shall have it all,” said the little man, reached into the bush, and — only think — there lay fiddle and fowling piece in readiness, as though they had been ordered beforehand.
sentences.n: “denk einer” — let one think — is an old exclamation thrown into the narration: just imagine. bestellt wären is past subjunctive, as if they had been ordered. The 1857 text prints no comma before sprach here.

sentences.t: Er gab sie dem Knecht und sprach „was du dir immer erbitten wirst, kein Mensch auf der Welt soll dirs abschlagen.“
sentences.l: He gave them to the servant and spoke “whatever you may ask for yourself, no person in the world shall refuse it to you.”
sentences.i: He gave them to the servant and said: “Whatever you ask for, no one in the world shall refuse you.”
sentences.n: “was … immer” is was immer, whatever, pulled apart. sich erbitten is to ask for oneself. dirs = dir es.

sentences.t: „Herz, was begehrst du nun?“ sprach der Knecht zu sich selber und zog lustig weiter.
sentences.l: “Heart, what do you desire now?” spoke the servant to himself and moved merrily on.
sentences.i: “Heart, what more do you desire?” said the servant to himself, and went merrily on his way.
sentences.n: He addresses his own heart as du. begehren, to desire, is an elevated word. weiterziehen is separable.

sentences.t: Bald darauf begegnete er einem Juden mit einem langen Ziegenbart, der stand und horchte auf den Gesang eines Vogels, der hoch oben in der Spitze eines Baumes saß.
sentences.l: Soon after that he met a Jew with a long goat’s-beard, who stood and listened to the song of a bird that sat high up in the top of a tree.
sentences.i: Soon afterwards he met a Jew with a long goat’s beard, standing and listening to the song of a bird that sat high up in the top of a tree.
sentences.n: The Ziegenbart, goat’s beard, is the tale’s first stroke of caricature: a stock piece of period antisemitic cartooning fixed on the man before he has said a word. begegnen takes the dative, einem Juden; horchen auf is to listen to.

sentences.t: „Gottes Wunder!“ rief er aus, „so ein kleines Thier hat so eine grausam mächtige Stimme!
sentences.l: “God’s wonder!” he cried out, “such a small creature has such a cruelly mighty voice!
sentences.i: “God’s wonder!” he cried out. “So small a creature, and such a monstrous powerful voice!
sentences.n: ausrufen is separable. grausam, properly cruel, is used here as an intensifying adverb: dreadfully, monstrously. Thier is the 1857 spelling of Tier.

sentences.t: wenns doch mein wäre!
sentences.l: if it were only mine!
sentences.n: A wish with no main clause at all, carried by the subjunctive wäre and the little word doch: if only. mein stands alone as the possessive pronoun, mine. wenns = wenn es.

sentences.t: wer ihm doch Salz auf den Schwanz streuen könnte!“
sentences.l: if only someone could strew salt on its tail!”
sentences.i: if only somebody could put salt on its tail!”
sentences.n: “wer … könnte,” with the subjunctive and no antecedent, is a wish for an unnamed somebody: if only one could. The belief that a bird can be caught by strewing salt on its tail is as proverbial in German as in English.

sentences.t: „Wenns weiter nichts ist,“ sprach der Knecht, „der Vogel soll bald herunter sein,“
sentences.l: “If that is nothing more,” spoke the servant, “the bird shall soon be down,”
sentences.i: “If that is all,” said the servant, “the bird shall soon be down,”
sentences.n: “wenns weiter nichts ist” is if it is nothing more than that. “herunter sein” is to be down, with the direction word standing in for a verb of motion.

sentences.t: legte an und traf aufs Haar, und der Vogel fiel herab in die Dornhecken.
sentences.l: took aim and hit to a hair, and the bird fell down into the thorn hedges.
sentences.i: he took his aim, hit the mark exactly, and the bird fell down into the thorn hedge.
sentences.n: anlegen, to level a gun and take aim, is separable, with the an at the end. “aufs Haar” is to a hair, exactly. The Dornhecke is the thorn hedge that gives the tale its title; Dorn here is the thornbush as a whole, not one single thorn.

sentences.t: „Geh, Spitzbub,“ sagte er zum Juden, „und hol dir den Vogel heraus.“
sentences.l: “Go, rogue,” said he to the Jew, “and fetch the bird out for yourself.”
sentences.i: “Go on, rogue,” he said to the Jew, “and fetch the bird out for yourself.”
sentences.n: Spitzbub (also Spitzbube) is a rogue, a sharper. The servant abuses him at the first word between them, with nothing in the tale to provoke it. herausholen is separable; “hol dir” has the dative of advantage, fetch it for yourself.

sentences.t: „Mein,“ sprach der Jude, „laß der Herr den Bub weg, so kommt ein Hund gelaufen; ich will mir den Vogel auflesen, weil ihr ihn doch einmal getroffen habt,“
sentences.l: “Why,” spoke the Jew, “let the master leave the ‘bub’ off, and a dog comes running; I will pick the bird up for myself, since you have hit it once and for all,”
sentences.i: “Why now,” said the Jew, “let the master leave the ‘bub’ off — then a dog comes running; I will pick the bird up for myself, since you have hit it after all,”
sentences.n: A pun English cannot carry: take the Bub off the end of Spitzbub and what is left is Spitz, the name of a breed of dog — so if the master drops the Bub, a dog comes running. “laß der Herr” is the old deferential third person used upward instead of ihr, and the tale gives it to him throughout: let the master leave off. auflesen, to pick up, is separable. “doch einmal” is in any case, once and for all.

sentences.t: legte sich auf die Erde und fieng an sich in den Busch hinein zu arbeiten.
sentences.l: laid himself on the earth and began to work himself into the bush.
sentences.i: lay down on the ground and began to work his way into the bush.
sentences.n: “sich hinein arbeiten,” to work oneself in, has the zu of the infinitive slipped inside the separable verb — hinein zu arbeiten — and 1857 prints it as three words.

sentences.t: Wie er nun mitten in dem Dorn steckte, plagte der Muthwille den guten Knecht, daß er seine Fidel abnahm und anfieng zu geigen.
sentences.l: When he now stuck in the middle of the thornbush, wantonness plagued the good servant, so that he took his fiddle off and began to fiddle.
sentences.i: When he was fairly stuck in the middle of the thornbush, mischief so plagued the good servant that he took down his fiddle and began to play.
sentences.n: Der Muthwille (modern Mutwille) is deliberate mischief done for the pleasure of it, and the tale names it plainly as the whole of the servant’s motive: nothing has been done to him. It goes on calling him “der gute Knecht” all the same. Wie here is as, when; abnehmen is separable.

sentences.t: Gleich fieng auch der Jude an die Beine zu heben und in die Höhe zu springen: und je mehr der Knecht strich, desto besser gieng der Tanz.
sentences.l: At once the Jew too began to lift his legs and to spring up into the height: and the more the servant drew the bow, the better the dance went.
sentences.i: At once the Jew too began to lift his legs and leap into the air; and the more the servant drew his bow, the better the dance went.
sentences.n: je … desto, the paired comparatives: the more … the better. strich is streichen again, of the bow. The dancing is not the man’s doing — the fiddle compels everything that hears it.

sentences.t: Aber die Dörner zerrissen ihm den schäbigen Rock, kämmten ihm den Ziegenbart und stachen und zwickten ihn am ganzen Leib.
sentences.l: But the thorns tore his shabby coat, combed his goat’s beard for him and pricked and pinched him on his whole body.
sentences.i: But the thorns tore his shabby coat, combed out his goat’s beard, and pricked and pinched him all over his body.
sentences.n: Dörner is the older plural of Dorn, modern Dornen. The two datives ihm are datives of possession: his coat, his beard. The beard is brought back for the combing, and the injury is played for comedy.

sentences.t: „Mein,“ rief der Jude, „was soll mir das Geigen! laß der Herr das Geigen, ich begehre nicht zu tanzen.“
sentences.l: “Why,” cried the Jew, “what is the fiddling to me! let the master leave the fiddling, I do not desire to dance.”
sentences.i: “Why now,” cried the Jew, “what do I want with the fiddling? Let the master leave off the fiddling; I have no desire to dance.”
sentences.n: “was soll mir das Geigen” is what is the fiddling supposed to do for me, what good is it to me. das Geigen is the infinitive used as a noun, the fiddling. “laß der Herr” is the deferential third person again.

sentences.t: Aber der Knecht hörte nicht darauf und dachte „du hast die Leute genug geschunden, nun soll dirs die Dornhecke nicht besser machen,“
sentences.l: But the servant did not listen to it and thought “you have flayed people enough, now the thorn hedge shall not do better by you,”
sentences.i: But the servant paid no heed, and thought: “You have fleeced people enough; now the thorn hedge shall use you no better,”
sentences.n: schinden is to flay, and of people to fleece or bleed dry. The servant states the stock accusation against the moneylender as a settled fact, and the tale gives him nothing whatever to base it on: the caricature is doing the work a motive would otherwise have to do. dirs = dir es.

sentences.t: und fieng von neuem an zu geigen, daß der Jude immer höher aufspringen mußte, und die Fetzen von seinem Rock an den Stacheln hängen blieben.
sentences.l: and began afresh to fiddle, so that the Jew had to spring up ever higher, and the shreds of his coat stayed hanging on the spikes.
sentences.i: and began to fiddle afresh, so that the Jew had to leap higher and higher, and the shreds of his coat were left hanging on the spikes.
sentences.n: daß here is so that, introducing the consequence. “immer höher” is ever higher. “hängen bleiben” is to catch and be left hanging.

sentences.t: „Au weih geschrien!“ rief der Jude, „geb ich doch dem Herrn, was er verlangt, wenn er nur das Geigen läßt, einen ganzen Beutel mit Gold.“
sentences.l: “Oh woe is cried!” called the Jew, “why, I will give the master what he demands, if only he leaves the fiddling — a whole purse of gold.”
sentences.i: “Oh, woe is me!” cried the Jew. “Why, I will give the master whatever he asks, if only he will leave off the fiddling — a whole purse of gold.”
sentences.n: “Au weih geschrien” is the tale’s spelling of a Yiddish cry of distress (oy vey geschrien, woe is cried), put in the man’s mouth as a marker of foreignness and brought back whenever he is in trouble. “geb ich doch” — verb first, with doch — is an offer and not a question: why, I will give.

sentences.t: „Wenn du so spendabel bist,“ sprach der Knecht, „so will ich wohl mit meiner Musik aufhören, aber das muß ich dir nachrühmen, du machst deinen Tanz noch mit, daß es eine Art hat;“
sentences.l: “If you are so open-handed,” spoke the servant, “then I will stop with my music; but this I must say to your credit, you keep your dance up so that it has a style to it;”
sentences.i: “If you are so open-handed,” said the servant, “then I will leave off my music; but I must say this much for you: you keep up your dance in fine style;”
sentences.n: spendabel, free with money, is a jocular word. nachrühmen is to say a thing to someone’s credit, and mitmachen, to join in or keep up, is separable. “daß es eine Art hat” is a set phrase of approval: so that there is some style about it, properly, thoroughly. The compliment is paid for dancing the man was forced into.

sentences.t: nahm darauf den Beutel und gieng seiner Wege.
sentences.l: took the purse thereupon and went his ways.
sentences.i: thereupon he took the purse and went on his way.
sentences.n: The subject is not repeated; German lets it carry over from the speech tag. “seiner Wege gehen” is a fixed phrase with an old genitive, to go on one’s way. The tale calls this taking, not robbery, and the trial to come turns on that difference.

sentences.t: Der Jude blieb stehen und sah ihm nach und war still bis der Knecht weit weg und ihm ganz aus den Augen war, dann schrie er aus Leibeskräften, „du miserabler Musikant, du Bierfiedler: wart, wenn ich dich allein erwische!
sentences.l: The Jew stayed standing and looked after him and was quiet until the servant was far away and quite out of his eyes, then he screamed with all his bodily strength, “you miserable musician, you beer-fiddler: wait, if I catch you alone!
sentences.i: The Jew stood still and looked after him and kept quiet until the servant was far off and quite out of his sight; then he screamed with all his might: “You miserable musician, you beer-fiddler — wait till I catch you alone!
sentences.n: nachsehen, to look after someone, is separable and takes the dative ihm. “aus Leibeskräften” is with all the strength of one’s body. A Bierfiedler is a scraper who plays in taverns for his beer, the lowest rank of fiddler. wart is the clipped imperative warte.

sentences.t: ich will dich jagen, daß du die Schuhsohlen verlieren sollst: du Lump, steck einen Groschen ins Maul, daß du sechs Heller werth bist,“ und schimpfte weiter was er nur los bringen konnte.
sentences.l: I will chase you so that you shall lose the soles of your shoes: you scoundrel, stick a Groschen in your maw so that you are worth six Heller,” and abused him further with whatever he could get out.
sentences.i: I will hunt you till you lose the soles off your shoes! You scoundrel, put a groschen in your maw, so that you may be worth six hellers!” and he railed on with everything he could bring out.
sentences.n: The insult reckons a man’s worth in coin, and the arithmetic is meant to sting: swallow a whole Groschen and you are still worth only six of the smallest coins there are. The rate of Heller to Groschen varied from place to place, so the sum is an insult rather than a calculation. Maul is the mouth of a beast — of a person it is coarse, and it is chosen to degrade. “los bringen” is to get out, to bring out.

sentences.t: Und als er sich damit etwas zu Gute gethan und Luft gemacht hatte, lief er in die Stadt zum Richter.
sentences.l: And when he had done himself some good with that and made himself air, he ran into the town to the judge.
sentences.i: And when he had comforted himself a little that way and let off steam, he ran into the town to the judge.
sentences.n: “sich etwas zu Gute thun” is to do oneself a bit of good, to indulge oneself; “sich Luft machen” is to give oneself air, to let off steam. gethan is the 1857 spelling of getan.

sentences.t: „Herr Richter, au weih geschrien!
sentences.l: “Lord judge, oh woe is cried!
sentences.i: “My lord judge, oh, woe is me!
sentences.n: The cry from the thornbush comes back as the opening of his complaint.

sentences.t: seht wie mich auf offener Landstraße ein gottloser Mensch beraubt und übel zugerichtet hat: ein Stein auf dem Erdboden möcht sich erbarmen: die Kleider zerfetzt!
sentences.l: see how on the open highroad a godless fellow has robbed me and handled me foully: a stone on the ground might take pity: the clothes torn to shreds!
sentences.i: see how a godless fellow has robbed me on the open highroad and used me foully! A stone on the ground might take pity. My clothes torn to shreds!
sentences.n: “auf offener Landstraße” is the legal phrase — highway robbery is the charge, and it comes back word for word in the sentence. zurichten is to handle roughly, to knock about. “ein Stein möcht sich erbarmen,” even a stone might pity me, is an old lament. From here the complaint runs in verbless exclamations, the speed of a man in a rage.

sentences.t: der Leib zerstochen und zerkratzt!
sentences.l: the body pricked all over and scratched!
sentences.i: my body all pricked and scratched!
sentences.n: The zer- on both verbs means the thing is done all over and to pieces. German keeps the plain article, der Leib, where English needs the possessive: my body.

sentences.t: mein bischen Armuth sammt dem Beutel genommen!
sentences.l: my bit of poverty taken together with the purse!
sentences.i: my little all taken, purse and everything!
sentences.n: “mein bischen Armuth” — my bit of poverty — is what a poor man calls the few things he owns; Armuth (1857 spelling of Armut) stands for the little it buys. sammt is modern samt, together with. The tale hands him this poor man’s phrase and, in the very next breath, a purse of ducats.

sentences.t: lauter Dukaten, ein Stück schöner als das andere: um Gotteswillen, laßt den Menschen ins Gefängnis werfen.“
sentences.l: nothing but ducats, one piece finer than the other: for God’s sake, have the fellow thrown into prison.”
sentences.i: nothing but ducats, one piece finer than the last! For God’s sake, have the man thrown into prison!”
sentences.n: lauter is nothing but. Gold lovingly counted over in the same breath as the “bit of poverty” is the tale’s stock joke against him — the miserliness is the caricature, not something the man has done. “laßt … werfen,” lassen with a bare infinitive, is have him thrown.

sentences.t: Sprach der Richter „wars ein Soldat, der dich mit seinem Säbel so zugerichtet hat?“
sentences.l: Spoke the judge “was it a soldier who handled you so with his sabre?”
sentences.i: Said the judge: “Was it a soldier who used you so with his sabre?”
sentences.n: The verb stands first — “Sprach der Richter” — an old narrative turn that gives the sentence a chronicle-like ring. wars = war es.

sentences.t: „Gott bewahr!“ sagte der Jude, „einen nackten Degen hat er nicht gehabt, aber ein Rohr hat er gehabt auf dem Buckel hängen und eine Geige am Hals; der Bösewicht ist leicht zu erkennen.“
sentences.l: “God preserve us!” said the Jew, “a naked blade he did not have, but a gun he had hanging on his back and a fiddle at his neck; the villain is easy to recognise.”
sentences.i: “God forbid!” said the Jew. “He had no naked blade, but he had a gun hanging on his back and a fiddle at his neck; the villain is easy to know again.”
sentences.n: “ein nackter Degen” is a sword out of its scabbard, drawn. Rohr is again the barrel and so the gun itself; Buckel is the back, the hump of the shoulders. “hat er hängen” is haben with a bare infinitive of position: he had it hanging.

sentences.t: Der Richter schickte seine Leute nach ihm aus, die fanden den guten Knecht, der ganz langsam weiter gezogen war, und fanden auch den Beutel mit Gold bei ihm.
sentences.l: The judge sent his people out after him; they found the good servant, who had moved on quite slowly, and found the purse of gold on him too.
sentences.i: The judge sent his men out after him, and they found the good servant, who had gone on his way quite slowly, and found the purse of gold on him as well.
sentences.n: ausschicken is separable, and “nach jemand schicken” is to send for someone. The narrator still calls him “der gute Knecht,” and goes on calling him that through the trial and up the ladder.

sentences.t: Als er vor Gericht gestellt wurde, sagte er „ich habe den Juden nicht angerührt und ihm das Geld nicht genommen, er hat mirs aus freien Stücken angeboten, damit ich nur aufhörte zu geigen, weil er meine Musik nicht vertragen konnte.“
sentences.l: When he was set before the court, he said “I have not touched the Jew and have not taken the money from him, he offered it me of free pieces, only so that I should stop fiddling, because he could not bear my music.”
sentences.i: When he was brought before the court he said: “I never touched the Jew and did not take the money from him; he offered it to me of his own accord, only that I should stop fiddling, because he could not bear my music.”
sentences.n: “aus freien Stücken” is of one’s own accord, freely. anrühren is to touch, to lay a hand on. The defence is true to the letter — the purse was offered — and leaves out that the man was made to dance in a thornbush until he bled.

sentences.t: „Gott bewahr!“ schrie der Jude, „der greift die Lügen wie Fliegen an der Wand.“
sentences.l: “God preserve us!” screamed the Jew, “that one catches lies like flies on the wall.”
sentences.i: “God forbid!” screamed the Jew. “He snatches lies the way one snatches flies off a wall.”
sentences.n: “die Lügen wie Fliegen an der Wand greifen” is to catch lies as one catches flies on a wall — to pluck them out of the air by the handful. der at the head is the demonstrative: that fellow there. The odd simile is one more mark of foreign speech hung on him, along with Mein, au weih and the deferential “laß der Herr.”

sentences.t: Aber der Richter glaubte es auch nicht und sprach „das ist eine schlechte Entschuldigung, das thut kein Jude,“
sentences.l: But the judge did not believe it either and spoke “that is a poor excuse, no Jew does that,”
sentences.i: But the judge did not believe it either, and said: “That is a poor excuse; no Jew does such a thing,”
sentences.n: “das thut kein Jude” — no Jew gives money away — is the tale’s stereotype spoken from the bench as if it were law, and it is what decides the case: the servant is condemned because the story takes for granted that a Jew would never part with money freely. thut is the 1857 spelling of tut.

sentences.t: und verurtheilte den guten Knecht, weil er auf offener Straße einen Raub begangen hätte, zum Galgen.
sentences.l: and condemned the good servant, because he had committed a robbery on the open road, to the gallows.
sentences.i: and condemned the good servant to the gallows for having committed robbery on the open highway.
sentences.n: The frame is stretched wide — “verurtheilte … zum Galgen” — with the whole reason wedged inside it, which English cannot do. hätte is subjunctive: the ground as the court states it, not as the narrator vouches for it. Robbery on the highway was a hanging matter.

sentences.t: Als er aber abgeführt ward, schrie ihm noch der Jude zu „du Bärenhäuter, du Hundemusikant, jetzt kriegst du deinen wohlverdienten Lohn.“
sentences.l: But as he was led away, the Jew screamed after him “you bear-skin, you dog-musician, now you are getting your well-deserved wages.”
sentences.i: But as he was being led away, the Jew screamed after him: “You bearskin, you dog-fiddler, now you are getting your well-earned wages!”
sentences.n: ward is the old past of werden, modern wurde, here forming the passive. A Bärenhäuter, a wearer of a bear’s skin, is a byword for a ragged, slothful good-for-nothing; Hundemusikant is coined on the spot, a musician fit for dogs. “dein wohlverdienter Lohn” picks up the Lohn, the wages, that the tale opened with.

sentences.t: Der Knecht stieg ganz ruhig mit dem Henker die Leiter hinauf, auf der letzten Sproße aber drehte er sich um und sprach zum Richter „gewährt mir noch eine Bitte, eh ich sterbe.“
sentences.l: The servant climbed up the ladder quite calmly with the hangman; on the last rung, however, he turned himself round and spoke to the judge “grant me one more request before I die.”
sentences.i: The servant climbed the ladder quite calmly with the hangman; but on the last rung he turned round and said to the judge: “Grant me one more request before I die.”
sentences.n: hinaufsteigen is separable, the hinauf at the end. Die Sproße (modern Sprosse) is a rung: a man was hanged from a ladder set against the gallows. eh is the short form of ehe. The third wish is about to be spent, and the reader is meant to remember it.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ sprach der Richter, „wenn du nicht um dein Leben bittest.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” spoke the judge, “if you do not ask for your life.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” said the judge, “so long as you do not ask for your life.”
sentences.n: “um etwas bitten” is to ask for something; bittest is the second person singular. The judge guards against the one request he thinks dangerous, and grants the one that undoes him.

sentences.t: „Nicht ums Leben,“ antwortete der Knecht, „ich bitte, laßt mich zu guter Letzt noch einmal auf meiner Geige spielen.“
sentences.l: “Not for my life,” answered the servant, “I ask, let me play once more on my fiddle at the very last.”
sentences.i: “Not for my life,” answered the servant; “I ask you to let me play on my fiddle once more at the very last.”
sentences.n: ums = um das. “zu guter Letzt” is at the very last, as a final thing.

sentences.t: Der Jude erhob ein Zetergeschrei, „um Gotteswillen, erlaubts nicht, erlaubts nicht.“
sentences.l: The Jew raised a hue and cry, “for God’s sake, do not allow it, do not allow it.”
sentences.n: Zetergeschrei — from the old legal cry “Zeter!”, the shout that called the neighbours to witness a crime — is a shrieking outcry. erlaubts = erlaubt es, the plural imperative. He is the only one there who knows what the fiddle can do.

sentences.t: Allein der Richter sprach „warum soll ich ihm die kurze Freude nicht gönnen: es ist ihm zugestanden, und dabei soll es sein Bewenden haben.“
sentences.l: But the judge spoke “why should I not grant him the short pleasure: it has been conceded him, and with that it shall have its resting.”
sentences.i: But the judge said: “Why should I not allow him that brief pleasure? It has been granted him, and there the matter shall rest.”
sentences.n: Allein at the head of a sentence is but, however. gönnen is to allow a person something gladly, not to begrudge it. “dabei soll es sein Bewenden haben” is the formal phrase for closing a matter: there it shall rest. zugestehen is to concede, to grant.

sentences.t: Auch konnte er es ihm nicht abschlagen wegen der Gabe, die dem Knecht verliehen war.
sentences.l: Besides, he could not refuse it him on account of the gift that had been bestowed on the servant.
sentences.i: Besides, he could not have refused him, because of the gift that had been bestowed on the servant.
sentences.n: The third wish is quietly doing the work: no one can refuse the servant a request. verleihen is to bestow or grant, and the passive leaves the giver unnamed.

sentences.t: Der Jude aber rief „au weih! au weih! bindet mich an, bindet mich fest.“
sentences.l: But the Jew cried “oh woe! oh woe! tie me up, tie me fast.”
sentences.i: But the Jew cried: “Oh woe! Oh woe! Bind me up, bind me fast!”
sentences.n: anbinden, to tie up, is separable. He alone in the square has heard the fiddle before, and the cry is the only warning anyone gets.

sentences.t: Da nahm der gute Knecht seine Geige vom Hals, legte sie zurecht, und wie er den ersten Strich that, fieng alles an zu wabern und zu wanken, der Richter, die Schreiber, und die Gerichtsdiener:
sentences.l: Then the good servant took his fiddle from his neck, laid it right, and as he drew the first stroke, everything began to waver and to totter, the judge, the clerks, and the court-officers:
sentences.i: Then the good servant took his fiddle from his neck, settled it, and as he drew the first stroke, everything began to waver and totter: the judge, the clerks and the officers of the court;
sentences.n: “zurecht legen” is to lay a thing in place, to get it ready. Der Strich is one stroke of the bow, from streichen. wabern is an old word for a flickering, wavering motion, used chiefly of flame; paired here with wanken, to totter, it makes a general unsteadiness, though its exact force applied to people is a guess. alles here is everyone.

sentences.t: und der Strick fiel dem aus der Hand, der den Juden fest binden wollte:
sentences.l: and the rope fell out of the hand of him who wanted to bind the Jew fast:
sentences.i: and the rope fell out of the hand of the man who was going to bind the Jew fast;
sentences.n: dem … der is the correlative demonstrative and relative: out of the hand of him who. The dative dem marks the person the thing falls from, and German says the hand where English says his hand.

sentences.t: beim zweiten Strich hoben alle die Beine, und der Henker ließ den guten Knecht los und machte sich zum Tanze fertig:
sentences.l: at the second stroke all lifted the legs, and the hangman let the good servant loose and made himself ready for the dance:
sentences.i: at the second stroke they all lifted their legs, and the hangman let the good servant go and made ready to dance;
sentences.n: German uses the plain article, “alle die Beine,” where English needs their legs. loslassen and “sich fertig machen” are both separable. zum Tanze keeps the old dative -e.

sentences.t: bei dem dritten Strich sprang alles in die Höhe und fieng an zu tanzen, und der Richter und der Jude waren vorn und sprangen am besten.
sentences.l: at the third stroke everything sprang up into the height and began to dance, and the judge and the Jew were in front and sprang the best.
sentences.i: at the third stroke everything sprang into the air and began to dance, and the judge and the Jew were in front and leaped the best of all.
sentences.n: The three strokes are counted off like the three wishes, the three Heller and the three years — the tale keeps to threes throughout. “am besten” is best of all.

sentences.t: Bald tanzte alles mit, was auf den Markt aus Neugierde herbei gekommen war, alte und junge, dicke und magere Leute untereinander:
sentences.l: Soon everything danced along that had come to the market out of curiosity, old and young, fat and lean people among one another:
sentences.i: Soon everyone was dancing who had come to the market place out of curiosity, old and young, fat and lean, all mixed up together;
sentences.n: mittanzen is separable. “alles … was” is everything, meaning everyone, who. herbei kommen is to come up to the place, herbei pointing towards the speaker.

sentences.t: sogar die Hunde, die mitgelaufen waren, setzten sich auf die Hinterfüße und hüpften mit.
sentences.l: even the dogs that had run along set themselves on their hind feet and hopped along too.
sentences.i: even the dogs that had come running along sat up on their hind legs and hopped with the rest.
sentences.n: mitlaufen and mithüpfen, both separable, carry the mit that runs through this whole passage: along with the others.

sentences.t: Und je länger er spielte, desto höher sprangen die Tänzer, daß sie sich einander an die Köpfe stießen und anfiengen jämmerlich zu schreien.
sentences.l: And the longer he played, the higher the dancers sprang, so that they knocked one another on the heads and began to cry out pitifully.
sentences.i: And the longer he played, the higher the dancers leaped, so that they knocked their heads against one another and began to cry out pitifully.
sentences.n: je … desto once more. anfiengen is the 1857 spelling of anfingen, from separable anfangen.

sentences.t: Endlich rief der Richter ganz außer Athem, „ich schenke dir dein Leben, höre nur auf zu geigen.“
sentences.l: At last the judge called, quite out of breath, “I make you a present of your life, only stop fiddling.”
sentences.i: At last the judge cried, quite out of breath: “I grant you your life — only stop fiddling!”
sentences.n: Athem is the 1857 spelling of Atem. schenken is to give as a gift: the life is handed back as a favour, not as a verdict overturned. aufhören is separable, its auf at the end.

sentences.t: Der gute Knecht ließ sich bewegen, setzte die Geige ab, hing sie wieder um den Hals und stieg die Leiter herab.
sentences.l: The good servant let himself be moved, set the fiddle down, hung it round his neck again and climbed down the ladder.
sentences.i: The good servant let himself be prevailed upon, laid the fiddle aside, hung it round his neck again, and climbed down the ladder.
sentences.n: “sich bewegen lassen” is to let oneself be persuaded. absetzen, to set down or take off, is separable; hing is the past of hängen.

sentences.t: Da trat er zu dem Juden, der auf der Erde lag und nach Athem schnappte, und sagte „Spitzbube, jetzt gesteh wo du das Geld her hast, oder ich nehme meine Geige vom Hals und fange wieder an zu spielen.“
sentences.l: Then he stepped up to the Jew, who lay on the earth and snapped for breath, and said “rogue, now confess where you have the money from, or I take my fiddle from my neck and begin to play again.”
sentences.i: Then he stepped up to the Jew, who lay on the ground gasping for breath, and said: “Rogue, now confess where you got the money, or I shall take my fiddle from my neck and begin to play again.”
sentences.n: “nach Athem schnappen” is to gasp for breath. “wo … her” is the compound woher split across the clause. gesteh is the clipped imperative gestehe. The confession is got with the same instrument that emptied the market place.

sentences.t: „Ich habs gestohlen, ich habs gestohlen,“ schrie er, „du aber hasts redlich verdient.“
sentences.l: “I stole it, I stole it,” he screamed, “but you have earned it honestly.”
sentences.n: habs = habe es, hasts = hast es. The confession comes out under the threat of the fiddle, and it is enough. redlich — honestly — is the word the tale used in its first sentence for the servant’s three years of service.

sentences.t: Da ließ der Richter den Juden zum Galgen führen und als einen Dieb aufhängen.
sentences.l: Then the judge had the Jew led to the gallows and hanged as a thief.
sentences.n: lassen with two bare infinitives, führen and aufhängen, is the causative: had him led and hanged. The tale stops here, with no name for the man beyond “a thief,” no word about the gold he confessed to stealing, and nothing said of the servant, who keeps the purse, the fiddle and his life.

glossary.abschlagen: abschlagen — to refuse, to deny (a request); literally to strike off (infinitive, separable ab-)
glossary.bitte: die Bitte — request, plea (f.); also bitten — (I) ask, beg (1st sg.)
glossary.dabei: dabei — with that, alongside; also concessive, for all that
glossary.denk: denken — think (imperative sg.; “denk einer”: just imagine)
glossary.erhob: erheben — raised (3rd sg. past; “ein Geschrei erheben”: to raise an outcry)
glossary.es: es — it (neuter pronoun; also ‘he/she’ for neuter nouns such as das Kind, das Mädchen)
glossary.freien: frei — free (inflected; “aus freien Stücken”: of one’s own accord)
glossary.gefallen: gefallen — to please (“sich etwas gefallen lassen”: to put up with a thing)
glossary.guter: gut — good (inflected; “zu guter Letzt”: at the very last)
glossary.habs: habe es — have it (haben, 1st sg. present + es)
glossary.heller: der Heller — heller, the smallest copper coin (m.)
glossary.ihm: ihm — to him, for him; to it (dative)
glossary.ja: ja — yes; also a flavouring particle, surely, after all
glossary.mein: mein — my, mine; also Mein! — an old exclamation: why!, come now!
glossary.rohr: das Rohr — the barrel of a gun, hence the gun itself
glossary.schwerer: schwer — heavy, hard (inflected, dat. fem.; not the comparative here)
glossary.sorgen: sorgen — to worry, to fret (infinitive); also die Sorge — cares (pl.)
glossary.streiche: streichen — (I) draw the bow, stroke (1st sg. present)
glossary.strich: der Strich — stroke of the bow (m.); also streichen — drew, stroked (3rd sg. past; einstreichen: to pocket)
glossary.stücken: das Stück — pieces (dat. pl.; “aus freien Stücken”: of one’s own accord)
glossary.traf: treffen — hit, struck (3rd sg. past; of a shot)
glossary.wünsche: der Wunsch — wishes (pl.); also wünschen — (I) wish (1st sg.)
